newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Sprawling HK firms need management change.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sprawling HK firms need management change.

text.p: Savvy tycoons in freewheeling Hong Kong have used Asia's economic boom to build sprawling empires, but their family businesses and wheeler-dealer tactics may be ill-suited for a world of growing competition.
As Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule, the business world here is rapidly changing with mainland companies already up and running ahead of the handover on July 1.

Business consultants say Hong Kong firms will face growing competition from U.S. and European companies too, forcing them to refocus their businesses as Asian growth rates sober and bring on more professional management.
"The environment is changing for Hong Kong business," said Dr Neil Maxwell, managing director of Ernst & Young Management Consultants Ltd. "They do need to strategically look at their business."
COMPANIES HAVE STRAYED AWAY FROM WHAT THEY ARE GOOD AT
David Ng, managing partner Greater China at Arthur Andersen, said part of the problem for Hong Kong's family-run corporations was the enthusiastic drive of their founding members.
"Family people are entrepreneurs and their core competency is deal-making. Given the booming state of the Asian economy, there are so many things they can put their hands in," he said.

But while sealing a deal in telecommunications one day, shipbuilding the next and infrastructure the next may be considered a good track record, companies stray away from what they are good at, he said. "If they can't resist the temptation, they have a tendency to go into too many directions without really taking stock of what their core competency is."
"Sooner or later they are going to find that this will be a problem. They may become overstretched. They venture into areas that they are not good at," said Ng.

Business consultants said some companies in Hong Kong were no longer able to manage their diversity. "As companies become larger, management becomes more difficult," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in a recent report.
"Entrepreneur-dominated companies are hampered by decision-making bottlenecks."

Operating in a more competitive environment then becomes increasingly difficult, experts said. "We are going to find some of the business lines are not going to remain profitable," said Maxwell. "Probably they are going to be competing with the large international firms."
FAMILY-BUSINESSES SEEK PROFESSIONAL HELP
Gerry Hopkinson, a partner at KPMG Peat Marwick, said there was a global trend to go back to core businesses, with companies divesting operations which had become a burden on profitability.

"Five years ago it was very much 'we must be diversified and spread risk' and that sort of thing, but now it is going back to the so-called focus businesses," he said. "At the moment there is very much a retrenching phase that is going on -- going back to what you are good at."
Family-run companies are also turning outside the family network to professional management for strategic assistance.
"There is a realisation that in order to develop a business further it needs a different structure, it needs a different set of business skills," said Hopkinson.
As the family founder gets older, the search for a successor may also move outside the family circle.

"It is important to address the succession issue head on," said Ng. "This generation will be gone in another 10 years but a lot of the time the problem just gets swept under the carpet. This is as dangerous as planting a time bomb."
As family-run companies open their shareholder structure by listing their shares on the stock exchange, they need to adopt a more professional approach to management, experts added.
FAMILIES RETAIN CONTROL

But while professionals are being brought in to implement strategy decisions, entrepreneurs are keeping firm control of their companies with their family's network of business and political connections key to signing business deals.
"These connections are very useful, especially when it comes to opening doors and getting a foothold in specific sectors," said Ng.
Kenneth Lam, an audit partner at Price Waterhouse, said some businesses are benefiting from both worlds, sending their second generation successors to business schools.

"The second generation, most of them would have been educated overseas and they are more open to new ideas," he said. "They have now expanded the network. They benefit from the old network and are receptive to new management concepts."
